references.text: Describes which crops were destroyed by the hail—the flax and barley were struck down, while the wheat and spelt survived because they mature later.
The psalm describes how God destroyed the Israelites' enemies in Egypt with hail that struck down the vine trees and sycamore trees, and killed the livestock.
A poetic retelling of the plague of hail where God sent hail and lightning that struck down vines and fig trees and shattered the trees in the land.
The plague of locusts that followed the plague of hail, where the locusts ate everything left after the hail—all plants and fruit on the trees.
God's command to Moses to stretch out his hand toward the sky to send hail over all Egypt describes a hailstorm mixed with fire.
John's Revelation describes hail and fire mixed with blood being thrown onto the earth, burning up a third of the trees and all green grass—a parallel to Egypt's plague of hail.
Great hailstones, each weighing about a talent, fall from heaven upon people—an eschatological parallel to the plague of hail in Egypt.
The locusts complete the destruction of everything left by the hail, emphasizing God's total sovereignty over Egypt's nature.
The swarm of locusts comes as the immediate follow-up to the hail to finish destroying the land's crops.
Thematic parallel: Heavenly judgment that strikes both the population, animals, and the land's crops completely.
Parallel in the totality of judgment: Both events describe an extermination of all life (humans and animals) within a defined area.
Theological contrast/parallel: Total destruction in the flood versus selective judgment in Egypt where God's people are spared.
